title: Small Bob Pasta Dough
headnote: “Making pasta dough works best on a room temperature surface (like a big wood cutting board). Be careful with the water — you will most likely use a different amount every time due to egg size, humidity, flour quality, etc. Makes a little over a pound of pasta.” — Bob Mitchell

quotes.text: Making pasta dough works best on a room temperature surface (like a big wood cutting board). Be careful with the water — you will most likely use a different amount every time due to egg size, humidity, flour quality, etc. Makes a little over a pound of pasta.
quotes.span: “Making pasta dough works best on a room temperature surface (like a big wood cutting board). Be careful with the water — you will most likely use a different amount every time due to egg size, humidity, flour quality, etc. Makes a little over a pound of pasta.” — Bob Mitchell

items.raw: 1 tablespoon water, plus more as needed

steps.text: Combine the two flours and the salt in a large bowl, on a big wooden cutting board, or on a clean counter. Make a well in the center of the pile to hold the wet ingredients.
In a separate bowl, beat the eggs, olive oil, and 1 tablespoon of water well, then pour into the center of the well.

steps.lead: Work in the flour with a fork.
steps.text: Pull bits of flour from the inside wall of the well into the egg mixture with a fork, a little at a time, until the mixture is too thick to stir.
Work in the rest of the flour with your fingers. If the dough feels too dry, add water in small increments; if it is too wet and sticks to everything, add more flour.
Once the dough comes together, form it into a ball and knead vigorously for 10 minutes, until smooth and elastic.
Wrap or cover the dough and chill it in the refrigerator for 20 to 45 minutes.

Roll by hand with a rolling pin, or through a pasta machine, to the thickness you want. On a machine, start at the widest setting and work down one notch at a time; go to the thinnest setting for ravioli and tortellini.
Cook in boiling salted water with a splash of olive oil for 3 to 4 minutes, until the pasta floats to the top. Drain and add to your favorite dish.

notes.label: Best with
notes.text: creamy pasta dishes (cacio e pepe, carbonara, sage butter, clams and hot sausage, truffle and butter), ravioli, and lasagna.

notes.label: Weighing
notes.text: the gram amounts are conversions of Bob’s cup measures. Use them as a starting point and adjust with water or flour by feel, as he says.

notes.label: Ahead of time
notes.text: the wrapped dough keeps 1 day in the refrigerator. Cut pasta can be frozen in loose nests on a sheet pan, then bagged, for 1 month; cook from frozen.

notes.label: Filled pasta
notes.text: one batch is enough for the Ricotta Ravioli or the Tortellini in this chapter.

openQuestion: This is Bob Mitchell’s “Eggy Pasta Dough.” Is Bob the Small Bob this dough is named for? If Small Bob is someone else, or his dough is different, tell me.
